title: Open question: are light sins venial by nature, or only by God’s kindness?
source_text: X. Caeterum quamvis Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae communi consensu doceant, esse peccata quaedam leviora, quae cum vera justitia & sanctitate simul stant; & hominis amicitiam cum Deo non dissolvunt, nec hominem involvunt reatu poenae & mortis aeternae; ac propterea dicuntur peccata venialia: alia vero graviora, quae hominem statim ex justo injustum constituunt, illumque Deo inimicum reddunt, ac proinde morti & poenae aeternae obnoxium, ideoque vocantur peccata mortalia: Nihilominus inter eos non omnino certum & definitum est, An peccata illa leviora id habeant ex natura sua, & talia per se sint, ut justitiae divinae repugnet illa ad mortem aeternam imputare, & propter illa hominem in perpetuum & prorsus abjicere; cum propter levitatem suam, non nisi poenam & iram temporalem juste mereri possint: An vero per se quidem possent juste puniri perpetua a Dei regno exclusione, & sempiternis gehennae ignibus & cruciatibus; sed quod ad tantam poenam non imputentur, verum ad temporalem duntaxat, id referendum esse ad Dei voluntatem atque benignitatem, quae solum gravioribus & atrocioribus peccatis mortis aeternae poenam lege sua constituit: levioribus autem supplicia tantum quaedam temporalia in lege sua minatur, & reipsa infligit, cum si stricto jure uti ipsi liberet, longe severius & acerbius posset cum homine agere.
pass_a_gloss: But although the doctors of the Roman Church teach by common consent that there are certain lighter sins which stand together with true righteousness and holiness, and do not dissolve a person’s friendship with God, nor involve him in the guilt of eternal punishment and death, and are therefore called venial sins; but others graver, which at once constitute a person unjust from just, and render him God’s enemy, and therefore liable to eternal death and punishment, and are therefore called mortal sins: nevertheless it is not altogether certain and defined among them whether those lighter sins have that from their own nature, and are such of themselves, that it fights against divine justice to impute them to eternal death and for their sake to cast a person off forever and utterly—since because of their lightness they can justly merit only temporal punishment and wrath; or whether of themselves indeed they could justly be punished with perpetual exclusion from God’s kingdom and with the everlasting fires and torments of gehenna, but that they are not imputed to so great a punishment, but only to a temporal one, is to be referred to God’s will and kindness, which by His law has appointed the punishment of eternal death only for graver and more atrocious sins, but for lighter ones threatens in His law only certain temporal penalties and actually inflicts them, although if it pleased Him to use strict right He could deal with the person far more severely and bitterly.
pass_b_english: Romans agree on lighter vs. graver sins in effect—yet divide on whether light faults are venial by nature or only by God’s milder law.
Some hold eternal damnation for them would clash with justice; others that God could damn them strictly but chooses temporal penalties.
